sources.title: Spider-Man: conheça os 6 principais jogos do Homem-Aranha
sources.text: Muitos personagens dos quadrinhos ganharam destaque nos videogames ao longo dos anos, mas não dá para negar que nosso querido Homem-Aranha é um dos mais emblemáticos. Desde os tempos do Atari, no início dos anos 1980, o herói já ganhou dezenas de adaptações, para todo tipo de plataforma e com resultados muito variados. Por muito tempo, os jogos do Aranha oscilaram entre aqueles mais apressados para casar com o lançamento de filmes e experiências mais ambiciosas, que tentavam capturar o que torna o herói único: a sensação de balançar entre os prédios de Nova York, a agilidade nas lutas e o peso emocional de ser Peter Parker. Nem todos os jogos, porém, ficaram na memória dos fãs. Alguns definiram o que se espera de um game do personagem, seja pela liberdade de exploração, pela fidelidade ao espírito dos quadrinhos ou pela qualidade da narrativa. Por isso, separamos os principais jogos do Homem-Aranha em ordem cronológica . Confira! Há inúmeros jogos inspirados no herói mais querido da Marvel, então optamos por listar os que são considerados os principais. Lançado pela Activision e desenvolvido pela Neversoft, o Spider-Man de 2000 foi o primeiro grande sucesso do herói na era 3D . Chegou ao PlayStation, Nintendo 64 , Dreamcast e PC, e apostou em uma história original que reunia parte da galeria de vilões do herói, como Doutor Octopus, Venom e Carnage, em uma trama inspirada em um desenho animado dos anos 1990. O jogo ganhou destaque também pela presença de Stan Lee, que aparece como ele mesmo na narrativa. O jogo ainda era linear, dividido em fases, mas transmitia bem a acrobacia e o clima de aventura de uma revista em quadrinhos. Para muita gente, foi a primeira vez que um game do Aranha realmente parecia à altura do personagem, e ele abriu caminho para o que viria depois. Baseado no filme de Sam Raimi, com Tobey Maguire no papel principal, Spider-Man 2 é lembrado até hoje como um dos maiores marcos da franquia , e o motivo tem nome: liberdade. Desenvolvido pela Treyarch, o jogo colocou o jogador em uma Nova York aberta, que podia ser explorada livremente, com missões paralelas, criminosos aleatórios para deter e cidadãos para ajudar. O grande diferencial era o sistema de balanço. Em vez de atirar teias em um ponto fixo do céu, o herói realmente se prendia aos edifícios, com controles que davam a sensação de física e de peso. Até hoje, muitos fãs afirmam que essa foi uma das melhores representações do movimento do Aranha até a chegada da nova geração de jogos. Tobey Maguire e Alfred Molina, o Doutor Octopus, emprestaram suas vozes aos personagens , o que reforçou a ligação com o filme. Também desenvolvido pela Treyarch, Web of Shadows adotou um tom mais sombrio e maduro que os títulos anteriores . A história mostra Nova York invadida por criaturas simbióticas, e o jogador precisa lidar com a ameaça enquanto se relaciona com aliados como Mary Jane, Gata Negra e Wolverine, além de enfrentar Venom. O ponto mais marcante era o sistema de escolhas. Ao longo da campanha, o jogador decidia entre o caminho do herói e a influência do simbionte, alternando entre o traje clássico e o traje negro, e essas decisões alteravam parte da narrativa e o final do jogo. O combate ágil, com combos aéreos e golpes em paredes, também ajudou a consolidar o título como um dos favoritos de quem cresceu na era do PlayStation 3 e do Xbox 360. Depois de anos de altos e baixos, o Homem-Aranha finalmente recebeu um tratamento de superprodução com Marvel’s Spider-Man, da Insomniac Games , lançado em 2018 para PlayStation 4. A história acompanha um Peter Parker já experiente, com oito anos de carreira como herói, tentando equilibrar a vida pessoal, o trabalho e a luta contra o crime enquanto uma nova ameaça, liderada por Mister Negative e envolvendo figuras como Kingpin e Doutor Octopus, ameaça a cidade. O jogo brilha por combinar quase tudo o que os fãs esperavam: uma Nova York detalhada, um sistema de balanço fluido e viciante, um combate inspirado nos jogos do Batman da série Arkham e uma narrativa emocional , que trata Peter e Otto Octavius com surpreendente profundidade. Vendeu mais de 20 milhões de cópias, ganhou uma versão remasterizada para PlayStation 5 e chegou ao PC em 2022, o que ampliou ainda mais seu alcance. Lançado como título de estreia do PlayStation 5, Miles Morales continua a história da Insomniac , mas troca o protagonista. Agora, o foco é o jovem Miles, que acaba de herdar os poderes de Peter Parker e precisa proteger o Harlem e sua comunidade durante um inverno rigoroso em Nova York. Sua identidade é marcada por habilidades próprias, como os ataques de bioeletricidade, chamados de “Venom”, e a capacidade de camuflagem. Com uma campanha mais curta que a do jogo de 2018, mas igualmente intensa, o título se destaca pelo carisma do protagonista, pelo tom mais pessoal da história e pelo visual impressionante para a época. A trama envolve a corporação Roxxon e o Tinkerer, e mostra que o legado do Aranha pode ser carregado por mais de uma pessoa. O terceiro capítulo da série da Insomniac chegou ao PlayStation 5 em 2023 e elevou a escala da franquia. Pela primeira vez, o jogador alterna livremente entre Peter Parker e Miles Morales , em uma Nova York ampliada, que agora inclui os distritos do Brooklyn e do Queens. As novas asas de teia e os túneis de balanço rápido tornaram a exploração ainda mais dinâmica. A história traz Kraven, o Caçador, e uma das versões mais fortes de Venom já vistas nos games , com Tony Todd na voz do simbionte, além do impacto do traje negro sobre Peter e de seu conflito com Harry Osborn. O jogo vendeu mais de 10 milhões de cópias e chegou ao PC em janeiro de 2025. É considerado por muitos o ponto mais alto da franquia até agora, tanto pela ambição da narrativa quanto pela evolução das mecânicas. Gostou de conferir os principais jogos do Homem-Aranha? stories.title: Epic Games delays Disney game and tells developers to go "AI first"
stories.summary: Epic Games has delayed its upcoming Disney collaboration - a shooter featuring characters from the Marvel and Star Wars franchises - and told developers to move to an "AI first" production model. Read more

sources.name: GamesIndustry.biz
sources.title: Epic Games delays Disney game and tells developers to go "AI first"
sources.text: The shooter featuring Marvel and Star Wars characters had been slated for March Epic Games has delayed its upcoming Disney collaboration - a shooter featuring characters from the Marvel and Star Wars franchises - and told developers to move to an "AI first" production model. According to Bloomberg , the game had been slated for March, but no new release date has been confirmed. People familiar with the project told the site that developers were asked to build the game with AI tools, including Anthropic's Claude, with staff overseeing the output. In an internal message seen by Bloomberg, one of the game's directors told staff: "No more hand-written code." The director also said all of the game's art would be "generated with full AI workflows." In a statement to Bloomberg, Epic communications director Jake Jones said the company is "embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do." Disney did not immediately respond to the outlet's request for comment. Developers were told about the change on a video call last week, and some were "stunned" according to Bloomberg's sources. The same sources also said development had fallen behind schedule, partly because Epic misjudged the staffing and time the game would need. Bloomberg noted that Epic was already encouraging AI use across its divisions, and said no other major games company has previously tried to make a game mostly with AI. Disney invested $1.5 billion in Epic in 2024 and took an equity stake , and the two companies announced a partnership covering multiple games, with this shooter due to be the first. In March, Epic said it was cutting 1,000 jobs , in part due to slowing engagement in Fortnite. A 2026 GDC survey found that more than a third of game developers use AI in their work , while more than half believe it is harmful to the industry. Earlier today we reported that Yuji Horii, the creator of Dragon Quest, had produced a new game using AI in about 30 minutes .

sources.name: Kotaku
sources.title: Epic Games Forces Shocked Developers Into ‘AI-First’ Mode For Delayed Shooter Featuring Marvel And Star Wars Characters
sources.text: Epic Games is rushing headfirst into generative AI-based game development for an upcoming Disney shooter that uses characters from Marvel and Star Wars. Developers on the project were reportedly told to implement AI in their workflows, including for producing the game’s art. According to a new report by Bloomberg , developers on the game were told to implement an “AI-first” production model using Anthropicâs Claude AI models. The team is not to use any more “hand-written code,” and even artists are being pushed to use the technology that has become a punching bag among actual players. The director of the unannounced game reportedly told developers that all art should be âgenerated with full AI workflows.â “Weâre embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do,â Jake Jones, communications director at Epic Games, said in a statement. Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney has made no secret of his love of generative AI, and even criticized storefronts like Steam for forcing developers to disclose their use of the technology on its store pages. But staff within Epic Games’ ranks have been less impressed. According to Bloomberg , many working on the Disney game responded to last week’s surprise AI policies with confusion and shock. It’s unclear what the company’s guardrails are for fixing mistakes made by AI and not letting “slop” seep into the final work product. The upcoming shooter, which Bloomberg reports was supposed to release in March 2027, has now been delayed due to slow progress and understaffed teams. Despite a $1.5 billion investment by Disney in 2024 for collaborations that include this project, the Fortnite maker laid off 1,000 people earlier this year amid the battle royale’s struggles and the costs of ongoing antitrust litigation. Modding and homebrew scenes have been overrun in recent weeks with an onslaught of new vibe-coded projects thanks to big improvements in the latest AI models like Claude Opus 5.5. It’s affected everything from jailbreaking PS5s to people being able to play versions of popular classics inside their browsers . As of yet, however, there’s been no major gaming company to try to utilize the technology on a massive scale as the foundation for its development pipeline. sources.name: Polygon
sources.title: Epic Games Delays Marvel and Star Wars Crossover Game Amid Generative AI Push
sources.text: Epic Games has delayed an unannounced game that would cross over Marvel and Star Wars characters in a shooter, according to Bloomberg . The Fortnite and Unreal Engine maker is now reportedly pushing the game's developers to use generative AI tools, like Anthropic's Claude, to complete development. The crossover shooter game was previously slated for March 2027, but is now without a new release date. "No more hand-written code," one of the directors on the game told staff, according to Bloomberg. Developers are now pivoting toward an "AI-first" development process, which includes having all art for the game "generated with full AI workflows," according to the director's message. Epic Games communications director Jake Jones told Bloomberg, "We’re embracing AI-accelerated development, led by Epic developers who are the visionaries and creative drivers for everything we do." Some Epic developers were reportedly shocked by the AI-first pivot. Shortly before Bloomberg published its story, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney said the company has a "huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration" in a statement on X . "The aim isn't to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal." Disney invested $1.5 billion in Epic Games in 2024, and also agreed to a multi-game partnership with Epic. The two companies collaborated to bring an AI-voiced Darth Vader into Fortnite last year, and players quickly abused it . This summer, Epic announced it would be using AI to voice three dozen Fortnite skins . The AI voices were trained on the performances of consenting actors in a situation that is not unlike last fall's Arc Raiders AI voice controversy . A user on X responded to Sweeney's post by saying the CEO wasn't reading the room well in terms of how people view AI use in game development. "Much of the room wants it to be 2016 again, but it's not," Sweeney responded . "Our job, as the provider of tools and technology to much of the industry, is to design for the present that is and the future that will soon be. Personally I'm optimisic [sic] about it and see it as empowering for creators." Epic Games and Sweeney's most recent championing of generative AI tools comes after the company laid off over 1,000 developers in March . Sweeney cited a "downturn in Fortnite engagement" beginning last year that led to Epic Games spending more than it was making. Bloomberg noted that development on the Marvel and Star Wars game has been slower than Epic expected as the company underestimated how many developers and how much time the game would need, according to Bloomberg's sources. On X, Sweeney engaged with other users who responded to his post with questions about game development. One user wondered , "How does this line up with firing 1000 people though." Sweeney did not respond to their question.

stories.title: Haunted Chocolatier 'More of an Action RPG' Compared to Stardew Valley, ConcernedApe Says
stories.summary: Eric Barone, aka ConcernedApe, has discussed the difference between his all-conquering indie game Stardew Valley and his hotly anticipated follow-up, Haunted Chocolatier.

sources.name: IGN
sources.title: Haunted Chocolatier 'More of an Action RPG' Compared to Stardew Valley, ConcernedApe Says
sources.text: Eric Barone, aka ConcernedApe, has briefly discussed the difference between his all-conquering indie game Stardew Valley and his hotly anticipated follow-up, Haunted Chocolatier . Barone announced Haunted Chocolatier back in 2021, but amid ongoing work on his phenomenally successful Stardew Valley, progress on the follow-up has been slow going. Indeed, in June, Barone admitted to feeling somewhat embarrassed to have to keep on saying he was still working away on the game. “Feels kinda dumb posting this same thing over and over, but that’s the reality,” he said at the time. In a new interview with GQ (thanks, Eurogamer ), Barone touched on what to expect from Haunted Chocolatier when it eventually comes out, and it sounds more different from Stardew Valley than I had expected. It’s set in a more “metaphysical” locale, for a start, and in terms of gameplay it’s more of an action RPG. “It is still what I call a town game,” Barone said, “But it’s more of an action RPG — the main focus is more about adventuring, finding equipment and getting more powerful. There are monsters, there are boss fights. It's for the people in Stardew Valley that go into the mines. That's what I do, honestly.” In June, Barone admitted fussing over every last detail in a bid to make Haunted Chocolatier as close to perfect as humanly possible . “I am being very thoughtful about every aspect of the game,” he said at the time. “The things in the game which the player will be interacting with or using very often need to be ‘perfect.’ They need to be seamless, clear, intuitive, satisfying, aesthetic.” He used the example of iterating on the recipe book for making chocolates, which sounded like a significant challenge. “To me, it’s not a simple task, as I torture myself over every last detail,” he said. “This is a UI you will be using fairly often, so it has to be perfect. You need to be able to accomplish your goal with the minimal number of clicks. There needs to be just the right amount of data presented to the player: not so much as to be overwhelming, but not so little as to be trivial or mundane. And the way that this data is laid out on the page is crucial… If the data is all clustered together, it will be disgusting to look at. The data needs to be grouped into compelling, intuitive and easy to read/understand groupings. It needs to look appealing and intriguing. And this is just the bare minimum, that players will likely take for granted. If all of that is accomplished then the player is now comfortable while perusing the recipe book. But I want more than just comfort. I want to delight the player. All of this typically requires me to iterate on something several times before I’m satisfied with it.” Barone also explained why he didn't want to show Haunted Chocolatier off too much at this stage of development. “Partly, it feels like I’m serving a half-baked bread. I would rather serve a fully baked bread,” he said. “Also, I know that many parts of the game will likely evolve and change before release, so if I reveal them early, I risk disappointing players if the final product does not match their expectation. Fortunately, I’m in a position where I don’t need to market the game, so I can take my preferred approach.” Haunted Chocolatier is so far without a release date, as is Stardew Valley 1.7 update, which Barone isn’t working on directly. Earlier this year, he explained his current way of working in an interview with IGN . “Well, part of the reason why I've expanded my team a little bit is so that hopefully I can spend more time working on Haunted Chocolatier," he told us in February. "And it's worked out pretty well so far, I would say. On 1.7, the approach we're taking is that I am like, you might say the creative director and I'm involved with like, 'Okay, here's what we're going to do. Here's some of the ideas.' Then I let the team work on that. And then meanwhile, I'm working on Haunted Chocolatier. "At some point in 1.7's cycle, I will get heavily involved, because I feel like my hand needs to touch every part of the game, every aspect of the update. I need to go over it and adjust it or at least approve everything. So it will require a lot of my time anyway, but I think the balance has been a little bit more shifted, so that I can spend more time focused on Haunted Chocolatier. And I think it's been working out pretty good. That's been a big change from the 1.3 update or 1.1 or something where it's completely me. I had no time to work on a new game. So that has changed. "It is difficult because it's hard to shift gears, I guess. If I'm thinking about Haunted Chocolatier, it's difficult to be like, 'Okay, I'm going to one day of the week or two days of the week work on Stardew Valley.' That's not how my brain works. I'm all in one thing or the other. So I've been trying to work on that. I feel like it requires a lot of discipline, which I'm always working to improve on." We interviewed ConcernedApe and chatted about topics such as the addition of two new marriage candidates with 1.7 , the one secret players still haven't found yet , and why there isn't a Stardew Valley TV show yet . We also chatted with the Stardew Valley community about what the game has meant to them over the years. Wesley is IGN's Managing Editor. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

sources.name: Eurogamer
sources.title: Stardew Valley creator's new game, Haunted Chocolatier, is "more of an action RPG" than farming sim
sources.text: "It's for the people that go into the mines." Stardew Valley creator Eric Barone, has given a new interview - and finally revealed a little more information about his upcoming title, Haunted Chocolatier. In a wide-ranging interview with GQ , which tackles topics ranging from creative burnout to the importance of 'cosy gaming', Barone also slips in some new information about what we can expect from his highly-anticipated Stardew Valley follow-up. And it's all rather surprising. Per the interview, this game is a much more action-oriented affair than the cosy homesteading of Stardew Valley: "It is still what I call a town game," he told GQ, "but it's more of an action RPG - the main focus is more about adventuring, finding equipment and getting more powerful. There are monsters, there are boss fights." For anyone that's played Stardew Valley, this won't be a massive shock; there is a combat element to the game, though mostly it's sequestered to one portion of the map - the mines that hold some of the game's rarest materials. If you had fun venturing in there at night to fight slimes and horde minerals, you're going to like Haunted Chocolatier, it seems. "[The new game] is for the people in Stardew Valley that go into the mines. That's what I do, honestly," said Barone. Elsewhere, Barone noted that Haunted Chocolatier is a more "metaphysical" experience than Stardew Valley - which makes sense, I suppose, given its connection to the world of ghosts and spirits - and that "no one's playing the game until I'm ready to show it". Hence, there's still no word on a solid release date. The last update we had on the game was all the way back in January, where Barone noted "I'm alive, the game is still in development" , following up previous statements he made alluding to the fact that the world of Haunted Chocolatier is bigger than Stardew Valley. As for when it's coming out? "The bottom line is, I don’t want to give a release date," Barone said at the start of the year. "The game will come out when it's done." If you want to learn more about the man behind one of video gaming's biggest phenomena of the past few generations, I'd urge you to read the full GQ piece: it's a sensitive, comprehensive look at a man that boasts many talents, yet is also humble and grounded. If you're interested in the musical side of his development process, I profiled Barone once in my column at The Guardian.

sources.name: GamesRadar
sources.title: Haunted Chocolatier is for the Stardew Valley players who yearn for the mines, ConcernedApe says
sources.text: Compared to Stardew Valley, ConcernedApe's next game is "more of an action RPG" Good news if you yearn for the mines in Stardew Valley – creator Eric "ConcernedApe" Barone says his long-awaited follow-up game Haunted Chocolatier is for you. In a new interview with GQ , Barone doubles down on an explanation he previously gave of Haunted Chocolatier – even though "it is still what I call a town game," we can expect this one to be "more of an action RPG." He's previously spoken about it having "a greater focus on combat," and he now elaborates: "The main focus is more about adventuring, finding equipment and getting more powerful. There are monsters, there are boss fights." It's the Stardew Valley comparison he makes that really speaks to me, though, and it sounds like Barone and myself have had a very similar experience with his first game. "It's for the people in Stardew Valley that go into the mines," he says. "That's what I do, honestly." There's still absolutely no word on when we can expect Haunted Chocolatier to launch. Back in August, he apologized that the game is taking so long , but said: "I won't compromise on the quality of the game by rushing it or releasing it too early. Then all my time would be wasted, anyway." This is a sentiment he's doubled down on now, too, saying: "No one's playing the game until I'm ready to show it. If you have a turkey in the oven. You're not going to pull it out halfway and have the guests taste it, right? It needs to be done." So, no Haunted Chocolatier food poisoning for us. Haunted Chocolatier is "way bigger than Stardew Valley," says ConcernedApe: "Everything is cranked up." stories.title: He-Man and the Masters of the Universe: Dragon Pearl of Destruction Release Date Confirmed
stories.summary: He-Man and the Masters of the Universe: Dragon Pearl of Destruction has a release date: February 4, 2027.

sources.name: IGN
sources.title: He-Man and the Masters of the Universe: Dragon Pearl of Destruction Release Date Confirmed
sources.text: He-Man and the Masters of the Universe: Dragon Pearl of Destruction has a release date: February 4, 2027. Bitmap Bureau, the developer behind Terminator 2D: No Fate, worked with Mattel and the retro team at Clear River Games on the old-school brawler, which launches digitally and physically on Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X and S. Two physical versions of the game will be available via Limited Run Games. The standard physical release costs $29.99, and the Collector’s Edition costs $99.99. Dragon Pearl of Destruction is inspired by the much-loved ‘80s animated series, and you can see that come through in pixel-art and 2D gameplay. The playable characters are He-Man, She-Ra, Man-At-Arms, and Teela, and you can play solo or co-op (two-player local co-op). There are 13 stages, including the Royal Palace, the Vine Jungle, and Snake Mountain, and famous villains such as Skeletor, Evil-Lyn, Beast Man, and Trap Jaw. You’ll also bump into the dark sorceress Shokoti and the Shadow Beasts. The Collector’s Edition includes lunchbox style packaging, pin badges, a mini-power sword, and an acrylic standee featuring He-Man riding Battle Cat, among other things. The contents of both physical editions are detailed below. We previewed He-Man and the Masters of the Universe: Dragon Pearl of Destruction in August and thought it could be the first ever good He-Man game. It comes following the release of Amazon’s Masters of the Universe, which struggled at the box office but found success on Prime Video. Wesley is IGN's Managing Editor. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

sources.title: He-Man and the Masters of the Universe: Dragon Pearl of Destruction launches February 4, 2027
sources.text: Side-scrolling beat’ em up game He-Man and the Masters of the Universe: Dragon Pearl of Destruction will launch for PlayStation 5 , Xbox Series , PlayStation 4 , Xbox One , Switch , and PC via Steam on February 4, 2027 for $29.99 / €29.99, publisher Limited Run Games and developer Bitmap Bureau announced. Physical edition pre-orders are available now via Limited Run Games . Here is an overview of the game, via Limited Run Games: Inspired by the iconic ’80s cartoon, He-Man and the Masters of the Universe: Dragon Pearl of Destruction allows players to take control of Eternia’s beloved heroes, including He-Man, Teela, Man-At-Arms, and more, to battle Skeletor and Evil-Lyn and save Eternia from plunging into darkness. Fight through over 13 action-packed levels using character-specific moves, abilities, and power-ups to stop Skeletor’s ancient ritual that threatens to take over Eternia. Battle Cat, He-Man’s fearless feline companion, also joins the fray, battling on the side of justice with his claws unsheathed.

sources.text: O grupo de supostos hackers Cyberleek publicou um novo vídeo vazado de GTA 6 que mostra Lucia, uma das protagonistas do jogo, explorando o mundo aberto completamente nua e saltando de paraquedas . A gravação tem cerca de cinco minutos e exibe diferentes elementos da jogabilidade não mostrados anteriormente pela Rockstar, incluindo combate corpo a corpo, interações com personagens e atividades em Vice City e outras áreas do estado fictício de Leonida. O vazamento, divulgado neste domingo (11), faz parte de uma série de publicações não autorizadas que vêm revelando detalhes do aguardado jogo da Rockstar Games, incluindo, também, o coprotagonista Jason pelado . Além das imagens recentes, o grupo ameaça divulgar uma versão funcional completa de GTA 6 , incluindo a campanha principal do início ao fim, caso uma meta financeira ligada a uma criptomoeda promovida pelos responsáveis seja atingida. A exigência apresentada pelo Cyberleek envolve também uma mudança na estratégia de distribuição do jogo: o grupo quer que a Take-Two Interactive, empresa controladora da Rockstar, reverta a decisão de não oferecer uma edição física de GTA 6 e publique um pedido de desculpas. Publicado no site descentralizado do grupo Cyberleek, o vídeo de aproximadamente cinco minutos de gameplay divulgado neste domingo (11) já se espalhou nas redes sociais. A gravação começa com Lucia dirigindo um veículo que aparenta ser um Vapid Hustler em Vice City, antes de sair do carro completamente nua, usando apenas um capacete durante parte das cenas. Apesar da situação inusitada, não há reações aparentes dos personagens ao redor, que seguem a vida normalmente mesmo com a protagonista sem roupa. O material também apresenta Lucia agredindo uma pedestre, com animações de combate corpo a corpo, e interagindo com um caixa eletrônico. Segundo especula o site TheGamer, a falta de reações dos personagens pode indicar que o modelo foi extraído de uma cena específica ou de uma ferramenta de depuração usada durante o desenvolvimento, em vez de representar uma possibilidade disponível normalmente no mundo aberto. Outra hipótese é que o vídeo mostre uma versão preliminar do jogo, na qual determinadas reações dos NPCs ainda não estavam implementadas. Na sequência, Lucia entra em um prédio, conversa brevemente com um trabalhador da construção civil e segue até um elevador. Depois de uma ligação telefônica, ela chega ao topo de uma estrutura identificada como AudaCity, recebe um paraquedas e salta em direção a um ponto de aterrissagem. As tentativas de pouso não saem como planejado: a personagem perde o controle da trajetória e colide com um edifício antes de morrer. Em uma segunda tentativa, ela chega mais perto do destino, mas ultrapassa o local indicado e cai no chão. O vídeo termina com um anúncio fictício da Buckme, que utiliza uma piada de duplo sentido. Como ocorre com outros materiais vazados durante o desenvolvimento de jogos, as imagens precisam ser interpretadas com cautela. Sem uma confirmação oficial da Rockstar, não é possível determinar com precisão qual versão do jogo aparece na gravação ou se todas as mecânicas exibidas estarão presentes na edição final. As imagens vazadas por Cyberleek também mostram mais detalhes sobre movimentações de dinheiro dentro do game. Em um momento, Lucia mexe em um caixa eletrônico, que exibe um limite de US$ 15 mil e a marca fictícia Buckme, enquanto a protagonista recebe US$ 23 após derrubar a personagem. No final do gameplay, também vemos o que pode ser um anúncio da marca Buckme, que inclui trocadilhos de cunho adulto envolvendo o nome do sistema de pagamento. O ponto mais preocupante da nova onda de vazamentos, porém, está fora da jogabilidade apresentada nos vídeos de Cyberleek. De acordo com o site especializado VGC , o Cyberleek afirmou que divulgará uma versão funcional de GTA 6 caso a criptomoeda associada ao grupo alcance uma capitalização de mercado de US$ 30 milhões. A promessa inclui a campanha completa, com a história jogada até o fim e os créditos finais. O grupo já havia utilizado uma meta financeira anterior para promover suas publicações e, agora, condiciona o vazamento de maior escala ao cumprimento do novo objetivo. A existência de uma versão funcional com todo o conteúdo prometido, no entanto, não foi verificada de forma independente. O Cyberleek afirma que a Take-Two tem uma maneira de evitar a divulgação: oferecer cópias físicas do jogo e publicar um pedido público de desculpas. A suposta justificativa apresentada pelo grupo é a insatisfação com a estratégia de distribuição de GTA 6, que prevê pré-vendas digitais sem uma edição física anunciada até o momento. A promoção de uma criptomoeda, entretanto, também levanta dúvidas sobre as motivações por trás da campanha. Anteriormente, na primeira onda de vazamentos, o grupo usou a imagem do jogo para valorizar a criptomoeda e realizou um grande saque de dinheiro antes de interromper os leaks. Com isso em mente, esse pode ser o plano novamente, aproveitando a expectativa em cima do lançamento do game. Neste domingo, a capitalização de mercado da criptomoeda Cyberleek estava em US$ 5,7 milhões, com cerca de US$ 17,7 milhões do ativo sendo movimentados por causa da nova onda de vazamentos. O grupo Cyberleek vem divulgando materiais não autorizados de GTA 6 há quase dois meses, incluindo vídeos que circularam antes de uma nova apresentação oficial relacionada ao jogo. Nesta semana, foram publicados aproximadamente 25 minutos adicionais de gravações, ampliando a quantidade de conteúdo disponível fora dos canais da Rockstar. A Take-Two já adotou medidas legais para tentar identificar os responsáveis. Entre as iniciativas estão pedidos judiciais de informações direcionados ao Discord, com o objetivo de obter dados relacionados a servidores e usuários que poderiam estar ligados aos vazamentos. A empresa também chegou a solicitar informações ao YouTube durante a investigação de contas aparentemente associadas à divulgação de vídeos não

stories.summary: Four characters and one stage will be available individually or as part of a season pass

sources.name: Video Games Chronicle
sources.title: Marvel Tokon’s Year One DLC roster confirmed, including Venom, Thor and Jubilee
sources.text: Four characters and one stage will be available individually or as part of a season pass The full Year One DLC line-up for Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls has been confirmed. As revealed during the EVO France fighting game competition this past weekend, a total of four characters will be coming to the game over the course of the next year, as well as one stage. The first to be added is Phoenix Cyclops, who was previously announced last week. He’ll be added to the game on November 2, it’s been confirmed. He’ll be followed by Thor (the Jane Foster version), who will arrive in ‘Winter 2027’. Because of the order the characters are listed, this likely means early 2027, rather than late in the year. Spring 2027 will see the arrival of Venom, as well as a new stage set on the planet Klyntar, the living prison created by symbiotes. Finally, rounding off the Year 1 DLC is X-Men teenager Jubilee, who will arrive in Summer 2027. All four characters and the Klyntar stage will be available to purchase individually, but a Year One pass will also be offered for those who wish to buy them all at a reduced price. Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls was released in August and was critically well received, with a current Metacritic score of 85. The game had problematic launch on Steam , however, with players reporting stuttering and inconsistent frame rates â something more forgivable in an action adventure game or an RPG, but not in a fighting game where expert players may study certain techniques on a frame-by-frame basis. Producer Takeshi Yamanaka told VGC in August that while he was “very appreciative” to see “a positive reception” to the game’s content itself, and among console players, the team was also well aware of the issues faced by PC players. “Currently, the team is hard at work on fixing these issues, and weâve now released two urgent patches,” he said at the time. “The CPU processing load issue has been greatly improved now as of the latest patch. However, the team is still hard at work to continue working on resolving remaining issues.”

stories.title: Sonic Racing CrossWorlds players demand Year 2 for free after noting the Digital Deluxe Edition promised ‘all future paid DLC’
stories.summary: The game's Year 2 paid DLC requires a second season pass

sources.name: Video Games Chronicle
sources.title: Sonic Racing CrossWorlds players demand Year 2 for free after noting the Digital Deluxe Edition promised ‘all future paid DLC’
sources.text: The game’s Year 2 paid DLC requires a second season pass A number of Sonic Racing CrossWorlds players have demanded that the game’s Year 2 content be made available as part of the Digital Deluxe Edition, due to the wording used when it was originally promoted. Sega announced the full details for Year 2’s upcoming content over the weekend, as well as a permanent price drop for the base game from $70 to $40 (and from $90 to $60 for the Digital Deluxe Edition). This includes another six packs of crossover content, which will be available either as separate payments or in a Year 2 Season Pass costing $29.99. Some players, however, have raised issue at the pricing for the Year 2 Season Pass, and are claiming they shouldn’t have to pay for it at all. Their reasoning, as noted by The Gamer , goes back to marketing messaging for the game before it was released, specifically a tweet posted in June 2025, three months before the game’s release on September 25, 2025. The tweet states that the Digital Deluxe Edition of the game includes the “base game, Season Pass, all future paid downloadable content and Sonic Prime characters”. Pre-Orders for the Digital Deluxe Edition are now live! This edition includes -Base Game -Season Pass -All future paid downloadable content -Bonus Sonic Prime characters Pre-order the Digital Deluxe Edition to also get -72-hour Early Unlock -Werehog Pack https://t.co/KIH4bEhMCc pic.twitter.com/YilRBo7e6q It’s the reference to “all future paid downloadable content”, and the fact it’s listed as a separate item from the Season Pass, which has had some players suggesting this means all the Year 2 content should be free too. At face value it appears the tweet was an unfortunately worded promise at a time when no further content may have been planned for the game beyond the initial first year. At the time of writing, however, it has not yet been removed. VGC has asked Sega for comment on the matter, and will update this article if it provides a response. Year 2 of Sonic Racing CrossWorlds starts on November 3, with the first paid crossover pack based on Godzilla. The six paid packs will feature the following crossovers: Free DLC content will also continue to be released for the game, including Bayonetta (on November 3), McLaren Racing (a new car and Sonic skin coming in late November) and Aigis from Persona 3 Reload (early 2027). Players who buy the Season Pass will get access to Genesis, Saturn and Dreamcast controller decal packs now, as well as vehicles based on each console when Year 2 launches on November 3. Players who own both Season Pass 1 and Season Pass 2 will also get Super Shadow and his Super Dark Flare vehicle as an extra bonus.

sources.title: Fans Accuse Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds Of Breaking Deluxe Edition Promise After Revealing FF7 DLC: ‘Paid $100 For This Sh*t, Guess I Learned My Lesson’
sources.text: Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds is a great racing game with a ton of post-launch support. Unfortunately, the balance between bombarding players with new content and how it’s been monetized hasn’t been equally impressive. Sega recently teased a collaboration with Final Fantasy VII and the rest of its year 2 DLC plans. The only problem is that fans who spent $100 on the Deluxe Edition will have to pay extra to access it. The game’s year 2 DLC roadmap kicks off on November 3 and was previewed over the weekend . It includes the following crossovers: Godzilla, Evangelion , Virtual Sanrio Puroland, Segaland, Midgar Pack, and Reload Revival Royal. Each pack is expected to add new stages and character skins, and the whole thing will cost players $40. Cloud racing against Sonic racing against SpongeBob? Sounds neat! Here’s why some existing players feel screwed. It goes back to a tweet Sega put out prior to Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds ‘ launch in June 2025. “Pre-Orders for the Digital Deluxe Edition are now live!” it read (via TheGamer ). “This edition includes: Base Game, Season Pass, All future paid downloadable content, Bonus Sonic Prime characters.” It’s that “all future paid downloadable content” that has gotten Sega in hot water and led their latest promotional marketing for year 2 DLC to get community noted on X. “All future DLC” is very different from just year 1 DLC, even if that’s what some people might have expected based on recent industry practices. “Paid 100 dollars for this shit, guess i learned my lesson,” one player wrote on Reddit. “Whether intentional or accidental, these DLC rug pulls have become increasingly common as online games become launch pads for mini-DLC storefronts. They’re especially common in fighting games when certain types of content gets promised at launch as being part of an initial expansion pass, only for a stage here or a character there to somehow drop out along the way . â¼ï¸ð£ï¸ https://t.co/eOpLkf2ONz pic.twitter.com/zgFkjkWJGd — Jibber Jabber (@JibbJabberish) October 12, 2026 Adding insult to injury is that some players already feel like too many of Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds crossover characters and stages were saved for the paid DLC. “It still pisses me off that the whole point of this game was that it was a crossover between different properties, but the game launched with only sonic characters and zero crossovers,” one fan wrote on the PS5 subreddit. “They started slowly adding Sega ones, but charging extra for anything that wasn’t already a Sega character.” We’ll see if Sega offers a make-good of some kind of just marshals on. The CrossWorlds DLC packs are usually $6, and players will have some time to make up their minds about whether to buy them. While the Godzilla pack arrives in early November, Evangelion doesn’t arrive until the start of 2027. Timing on the Final Fantasy VII stuff is still TBD. stories.title: Ex-Burnout devs came full circle for Star Wars Galactic Racer to bring the edge back to racing games
stories.summary: Fuse Games' Matt Webster and Kieran Crimmins join Lucasfilm Games' Craig Derrick to chat resurrecting the arcade racer

sources.name: GamesRadar
sources.title: Ex-Burnout devs came full circle for Star Wars Galactic Racer to bring the edge back to racing games
sources.text: Fuse Games' Matt Webster and Kieran Crimmins join Lucasfilm Games' Craig Derrick to chat resurrecting the arcade racer From the moment developer Fuse Games was founded in January 2023, the intent for the studio was to make a Star Wars racing game. CEO Matt Webster tells me that roughly three weeks into the studio's life, the team were on a plane to visit Lucasfilm Games and pitch the idea – "Galactic Racer". As a studio founded by former Criterion Games developers (Criterion Games previously helmed the Burnout series and later worked on EA's 2015 Star Wars Battlefront and its sequel), fusing the team's arcade racing pedigree and previous experience working on Star Wars titles, as Fuse's creative director Kieran Crimmins says, was "a no-brainer"). While 'Burnout but Star Wars' is certainly an intriguing pitch on its own (I was absolutely hooked on the concept from its first reveal in December 2025), the team at Fuse wasn't content with just going back to familiar territory when you need to stand out amongst a galaxy of games. Star Wars: Galactic Racer review : "True to its Burnout legacy, blisteringly fast space racing keeps me coming back to the grid" With series like Forza Horizon and Gran Turismo dominating the triple-A racing space, the focus has shifted from arcade action to realism and scale that makes the most of modern hardware. More cars, more tracks, vast open worlds, and endless rewards, for anyone and everyone. Even Mario Kart, one of the last mainstream bastions for arcade racing, followed suit with Mario Kart World's core feature being an open world. With their heritage and expertise from the arcade racing of the 2000s, the developers at Fuse Games were never going to follow the crowd when making Star Wars: Galactic Racer. "I think these guys at Fuse could've absolutely made just a killer arcade racing game," says Craig Derrick, executive producer at Lucasfilm Games. "But there was always the intention, I think from the very beginning, of "how do we push the genre forward?" It's not the first time the founders of Fuse have pioneered the genre either, with their previous work at Criterion Games partly shaping modern racing games too. 2008's Burnout Paradise – while not the first open-world racing game – undoubtedly went on to influence the first entries in the Forza Horizon and The Crew series, thanks to a map that lacked defined tracks and acted more as a driving playground. Crimmins describes this post-Burnout Paradise shift as a "sea change" but feels that there hasn't quite been another one in the racing genre since, despite there being plenty of polished racers across the triple-A and indie space. Specifically, he believes that consequences are "sorely missing" in big racing games, with Webster adding that some feel a bit toothless: "I think there's been a bit of a burnishing off of, I suppose, the edge in [racing games]. You put a car in the wall and what's going to happen? And if it's nothing, then it just falls a little bit flat from an emotional perspective." So, looking to make waves by bringing back consequence with Galactic Racer and after a lot of prototyping, the team at Fuse Games determined that the runs-based, roguelike-inspired format was the way to go. As I noted in my Star Wars: Galactic Racer review , I couldn't believe that this racing-roguelike hybrid had never been attempted before by a mainstream studio because it's a natural fit. Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more Applying a runs-based structure to an arcade racer fights against "a bunch of racing game conventions", explains Webster. As well as facing little to no consequences, players are also conditioned to win all the time in a lot of modern racing games, which is something that the roguelike mechanics in Star Wars: Galactic Racer vehemently oppose. "This game should challenge you, and we wanted to front that up, so you feel like 'a hard-fought fifth place? Yeah, I'll take it'," Webster says. Hurtling around Galactic Racer's circuits and inevitably obliterating your speeder means winning your first few events is unlikely, and it's an oddly refreshing humbling experience. Those crashes are also where Burnout's DNA shines through most in Galactic Racer. It also feels like classic Star Wars, which makes sense as Webster says that, in a full-circle moment, they were inspired by The Phantom Menace back in the day. "When we were making Burnout, the podracing sequence in Episode One was a massive influence in terms of the drama and the excitement and the sheer speed and power, and the visceral nature of those crashes was a big inspiration," he says. Bringing those back in a true Star Wars setting with a roguelike structure means each crash serves as a "learning moment" too, and, indeed, I quickly learned that survival is the priority, not victory. However, Galactic Racer was once a lot more punishing. Going over previous iterations of the wrecking out loop, Webster and Crimmins share that there was a version where you could crash only once instead of three times, and another where you had to finish in the top three every time – the latter lives on as the Eliminator event. Webster also says that Galactic Racer asks a lot from its players in terms of cognitive load . But it also went the other way, as Crimmins explains there was a version that was much more straightforward. "It felt like it lost all its teeth, and now it feels trivial, and my decisions don't matter," he says. "Getting that balance right is incredibly important to give you that emotional high when you do win but also give you that impetus to move forward when you don't." That's a doubly difficult balance to strike when a chunk of your audience might also just be in it for Star Wars with little to no experience with racing games. sources.title: After Burnout, Star Wars: Galactic Racer studio lead says "games should challenge players"
sources.text: The former Burnout developers behind Star Wars: Galactic Racer reckon it's important to challenge players, because they're going to tune out otherwise. Star Wars: Galactic Racer is a tough game. Intentionally so, with Fuse Games CEO Matt Webster saying "we are asking way more out of players" this time around compared to the Burnout games that a majority of the team used to develop, because "modern gamers can manage a greater amount of cognitive load." Not only is the racing extremely fast, but you have a slate of aggressive racers trying to ram you off the track, and the slightest hesitation on a turn can cause you to launch into a corner and explode. And given that you only have a finite amount of crashes before you're forced to forfeit, it's likely that some may take a significant amount of time before they even reach act 2. Speaking to GamesRadar+, Webster explains plainly: "Games should challenge players." With the Burnout series, he says, "we used to throw rewards at you – dopamine hits of reward, reward, car, car, car! Eventually, if that's just one note, then you start to tune it out." He adds, "But this game should challenge you. We wanted to front that up so you feel like, 'a hard fought fifth place – yeah I'll take it.'" Webster describes a need for what he calls "light and shade," calling the segments where you play as Shade when you reach a new planet an "important aspect." He says: "You've got the light and shade between the super high intensity racing and the lower intensity immersion in Star Wars." How former Burnout devs came full circle for Star Wars: Galactic Racer to bring the edge back into racing games: "'Arcade' is not the absence of depth." Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more Scott has been freelancing for over four years across a number of different gaming publications, first appearing on GamesRadar+ in 2024. He has also written for the likes of PC Gamer, Eurogamer, VG247, Play, TechRadar, and others. He's typically rambling about Metal Gear Solid, God Hand, or any other PS2-era titles that rarely (if ever) get sequels.
